matching.reasoningTemplate: Confusion or seizures with low sodium suggest symptomatic hyponatraemia — establish the mechanism before correcting.

clinicalPearls: Hyponatraemia (plasma Na+ <135 mM) is very common, affecting up to ~22% of hospitalised patients (p.390).
The absolute plasma Na+ concentration says nothing about a patient's volume status, which must be assessed separately for both diagnosis and management (p.390).

Hyponatraemia is almost always driven by excess circulating AVP and/or increased renal sensitivity to AVP combined with free-water intake; the main exception is hyponatraemia from low solute intake (p.390).
Diagnostically subdivide by ECF volume into hypovolaemic, euvolaemic, and hypervolaemic groups based on clinical history and volume status (p.390).
In hypovolaemic patients, a urine Na+ <20 mM predicts a brisk rise in plasma Na+ with isotonic saline, because AVP falls and a water diuresis ensues (p.391).
Serum uric acid helps discriminate: SIAD is typically associated with low uric acid (<4 mg/dL), whereas hypovolaemic hyponatraemia is often hyperuricaemic (p.391, p.393).
Thiazides can mimic SIAD and do not impair urinary concentrating ability, so AVP retains full effect; defer diagnosing SIAD until 1-2 weeks after stopping the thiazide (p.391, p.393).
The 48-hour mark distinguishes acute from chronic hyponatraemia and is decisive for how aggressively/cautiously sodium may be corrected (p.392).

Cerebral salt wasting (a rare hypovolaemic cause linked to intracranial disease) responds to aggressive salt-and-water repletion, so distinguishing it from SIAD is critical because their management diverges (p.391).
harrison.pathophysiology: Hyponatraemia reflects a relative excess of body water to sodium, almost always from increased circulating AVP (or heightened renal AVP sensitivity) together with free-water intake. Volume status modulates AVP release: hypovolaemia raises AVP at any given osmolality, and 'hypervolaemic' arterial underfilling (heart failure, cirrhosis) triggers neurohumoral activation that likewise elevates AVP, causing water retention. In hypovolaemia, AVP-mediated V2-receptor water reabsorption plus free-water intake lowers Na+. In hypervolaemic oedematous states (CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), total-body Na+ rises but water rises proportionally more; reduced arterial filling drives the AVP response. In euvolaemic hyponatraemia, SIAD is the commonest cause: free-water intake persists at osmolalities below the normal thirst threshold, with patients subclinically volume-expanded (so-called 'AVP escape' limits distal tubular transport, preserving a modestly hypervolaemic steady state). Four AVP-secretion patterns occur in SIAD: erratic unregulated secretion (~1/3 of patients), failure to suppress at low osmolality, a 'reset osmostat', and a subset with undetectable AVP (gain-of-function V2-receptor mutations causing 'nephrogenic' SIAD). At the brain level, hyponatraemia causes water to move down the osmotic gradient from hypotonic ECF into cells, producing cellular swelling and cerebral oedema within the rigid skull; acute encephalopathy results when volume-regulatory mechanisms (CSF shunting, efflux of Na+/K+/Cl-) are overwhelmed. In chronic hyponatraemia, brain cells extrude organic osmolytes (creatine, betaine, glutamate, myoinositol, taurine), a process largely complete within 48 h, which mitigates but does not abolish symptoms (p.390-392).
additionalDifferentials: Hypovolaemic: GI losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, tube drainage) and insensible loss (sweating, burns) with inadequate replacement — urine Na+ typically <20 mM (p.390).

Hypovolaemic renal: thiazide diuretics, mineralocorticoid/aldosterone deficiency (primary adrenal insufficiency, hypoaldosteronism), salt-losing nephropathies (reflux nephropathy, interstitial nephropathies, post-obstructive uropathy, medullary cystic disease, recovery phase of ATN) — urine Na+ typically >20 mM (p.390-391).
Osmotic/solute-driven hypovolaemic: glycosuria, ketonuria (starvation, diabetic or alcoholic ketoacidosis), bicarbonaturia (RTA, metabolic alkalosis) (p.391).
Cerebral salt wasting (subarachnoid haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, craniotomy, encephalitis, meningitis) (p.391).
Hypervolaemic: congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, and acute or chronic renal failure (the latter uniquely with raised urine Na+) (p.391).
Euvolaemic: SIAD, moderate-to-severe hypothyroidism, secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary disease (glucocorticoid deficiency) (p.391).
Low solute intake: beer potomania (alcoholics whose sole nutrient is beer) and nutrient-restricted/extreme vegetarian diets — urine osmolality <100-200 mOsm/kg, urine Na+ <10-20 mM (p.391-392).

SIAD causes: malignancy (especially small-cell lung carcinoma — 75% of malignancy-associated SIAD; ~10% present with Na+ <130 mM), pulmonary disease (pneumonia, TB, abscess, pleural effusion), CNS disease (tumour, subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis, encephalitis, head trauma, hydrocephalus), drugs, and transient causes (pain, nausea, stress, endurance exercise, general anaesthesia) (p.391-392).
Pseudohyponatraemia — hyponatraemia coexisting with normal/increased plasma tonicity, from extreme hyperlipidaemia or hyperproteinaemia (p.393).
Hyperglycaemia-related ('true') hyponatraemia — plasma Na+ falls ~1.6-2.4 mM per 100 mg/dL rise in glucose; resolves after correcting hyperglycaemia (p.393).
nonInfectiousMimics: Pseudohyponatraemia from severe hyperlipidaemia/hyperproteinaemia: measured Na+ is low but plasma tonicity is normal or high; exclude by measuring serum osmolality (p.393).
Hyperglycaemic hyponatraemia: a translocational, true hyponatraemia driven by glucose-induced water efflux that corrects once glucose is lowered (p.393).
additionalInvestigations: Serum osmolality, converted to effective osmolality/tonicity by subtracting urea (in mg/dL divided by 2.8) — true hyponatraemia has effective osmolality <275 mOsm/kg; this also excludes pseudohyponatraemia (p.393).
Serum glucose — to identify and correct hyperglycaemic (translocational) hyponatraemia (p.393).
Serum uric acid — low (<4 mg/dL) in SIAD physiology, often high in volume depletion (p.393).
Serum K+, BUN/creatinine — hyperkalaemia suggests adrenal insufficiency/hypoaldosteronism; raised urea/creatinine suggests renal cause (p.393).
Thyroid, adrenal and pituitary function testing, including a cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test to assess primary adrenal insufficiency, in the appropriate setting (p.393).
Urine osmolality — <100 mOsm/kg suggests primary polydipsia; >400 mOsm/kg indicates dominant AVP excess; intermediate values suggest multifactorial physiology (p.393).
Urine Na+ — <20-30 mM suggests hypovolaemia; >30 mM suggests SIAD, but values overlap, especially in the elderly (p.393).
Urine K+ — to calculate the urine-to-plasma electrolyte ratio, useful for predicting response to fluid restriction (p.393).
Demonstration that plasma Na+ corrects after isotonic saline hydration is the diagnostic gold standard for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia (p.393).
Imaging — chest CT in smokers/high-risk patients (screening CXR can miss small-cell lung carcinoma); CNS imaging where a central cause is suspected (p.393).
redFlags: Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia is a medical emergency: nausea/headache/vomiting can rapidly progress to seizures, brainstem herniation, coma and death (p.392).

Acute hyponatraemia can cause normocapnoeic or hypercapnoeic respiratory failure, typically from non-cardiogenic 'neurogenic' pulmonary oedema with normal wedge pressure; resulting hypoxia amplifies neurological injury (p.392).
Premenopausal women are far more likely than men to develop encephalopathy and severe neurological sequelae (p.392).

Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia (>8-10 mM in 24 h or >18 mM in 48 h) risks osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), classically central pontine myelinolysis — presenting days later with para-/quadriparesis, dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, 'locked-in' syndrome, or reduced consciousness (p.393).
ODS can occur even with appropriately slow correction in high-risk patients: alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, and liver transplantation (p.393).
Plasma Na+ <125 mM is the threshold at which chronic hyponatraemia commonly becomes overtly symptomatic (nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures) (p.392).

Iatrogenic settings for acute hyponatraemia: postoperative premenopausal women given hypotonic fluids, glycine irrigation (TURP/uterine surgery), colonoscopy prep, recent thiazide initiation (Table 56-2, p.392).
MDMA ('Ecstasy'/'Molly') causes potent thirst and AVP induction leading to severe acute hyponatraemia; exercise-associated (endurance/marathon) hyponatraemia is another acute setting (p.392).
harrison.prognosis: Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia carries high risk of severe neurological injury and death; encephalopathy is more severe in premenopausal women. The degree of hyponatraemia is an important prognostic indicator in hypervolaemic states, reflecting the intensity of neurohumoral activation. Chronic hyponatraemia, even when judged 'asymptomatic', is associated with subtle gait and cognitive deficits (reversible with correction), increased risk of falls, and an increased fracture risk due to neurological dysfunction and reduced bone density — so safe correction is warranted even without overt symptoms. Osmotic demyelination from overcorrection can produce permanent disabling neurological deficits (p.392-393).
pitfalls: Hypovolaemic patients may appear clinically euvolaemic, with only a low urine Na+ to reveal the cause (p.390).
Hyponatraemia is frequently multifactorial, especially when severe — evaluate every source of excess AVP (volume status, drugs, nausea, pain) rather than settling on one (p.393).
Failing to exclude pseudohyponatraemia/hyperglycaemia before correcting; check serum osmolality and glucose first (p.393).
The 93%-water assumption used by ion-sensitive electrodes makes plasma Na+ falsely low in extreme hyperlipidaemia/hyperproteinaemia (p.393).
Urine Na+ values overlap substantially between SIAD and hypovolaemia (particularly in the elderly); the saline-challenge response is the definitive discriminator (p.393).
Diagnosing SIAD in a patient on thiazides — defer the SIAD label until 1-2 weeks after stopping the drug (p.393).
Distinguishing cerebral salt wasting from SIAD is critical because management differs (salt repletion vs fluid restriction) (p.391).
harrison.severityClassification: By volume status: hypovolaemic (total body water down, total body Na+ down more), euvolaemic/no oedema (total body water up, Na+ near-normal), and hypervolaemic (total body water up markedly, Na+ up) — Fig. 56-5, p.391. By chronicity: acute hyponatraemia is <48 h (osmolyte extrusion incomplete, higher cerebral-oedema risk) and chronic is >48 h (osmolytes largely extruded, lower acute symptom risk but higher ODS risk on correction), p.392. By tonicity: true hypotonic hyponatraemia has effective osmolality <275 mOsm/kg, distinct from pseudohyponatraemia (normal/high tonicity) and hyperglycaemic translocational hyponatraemia, p.393. Symptomatic threshold for chronic disease is generally plasma Na+ <125 mM (p.392). SIAD diagnostic features include euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia, inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osmolality typically >400 mOsm/kg / not maximally dilute), urine Na+ >30 mM, low serum uric acid (<4 mg/dL), and absence of thyroid/adrenal dysfunction, diuretics, hypovolaemia or hypervolaemia (p.391, p.393).
